text:
Over the past decade, the Chinese government has systematically narrowed the space for independent reporting and autonomous civic activity through law, surveillance, coercion, and administrative control. The pattern is not incidental or localised: it reflects central political choices under Xi Jinping to subordinate information and association to Communist Party rule.

On press freedom, one of the most harmful developments has been the fusion of censorship with pervasive digital control. The Cyberspace Administration of China, together with propaganda authorities, has expanded requirements that news, commentary, and even private platform discussions align with officially approved narratives. Vague prohibitions on “rumours,” “picking quarrels,” and content that harms national honour or social stability give authorities enormous discretion. This causes harm not only by removing critical reporting after publication, but by inducing heavy self-censorship before anything is written. Editors, reporters, bloggers, and platform operators internalise political risk, which destroys investigative journalism and deprives the public of reliable information on corruption, public health, labour abuses, and disasters.

The crackdown in Hong Kong following the 2020 National Security Law is another major assault on press freedom. Although Hong Kong long had a distinct media environment, Beijing’s imposition of broadly defined offences such as subversion and collusion with foreign forces was used to shut down critical outlets, most notably Apple Daily and Stand News, and to arrest media owners and editors. The mechanism of harm here is legal terror: when ordinary journalistic contact with foreign organisations or criticism of government policy can be reframed as a national security threat, media pluralism collapses. Responsibility lies not just with Hong Kong officials implementing the law, but with the central authorities that designed and mandated it.

The treatment of civil society organisations shows a parallel strategy. The 2016 Foreign NGO Law placed overseas-linked NGOs under police supervision rather than a civilian regulatory framework. By requiring burdensome registrations, approved local partners, and extensive reporting, it made many forms of rights advocacy, legal aid, academic exchange, and community organising difficult or impossible. The harm is structural: organisations spend resources on political compliance, avoid sensitive work, or close entirely, leaving vulnerable groups with fewer avenues for support and fewer independent monitors of state abuse. Accountability rests with the National People’s Congress for enacting the framework, the Ministry of Public Security for enforcement, and ultimately the Party leadership that prioritised control over association.

Domestic civil society has also been weakened through targeted repression of lawyers, feminists, labour organisers, and rights defenders. The legacy of the “709” crackdown on human rights lawyers continued through surveillance, licence revocations, travel bans, arbitrary detention, and intimidation of families. Feminist activists and labour NGOs have been harassed or shuttered when their organising suggested independent social mobilisation. The mechanism is clear: by raising the personal cost of association to extreme levels, the state deters collective action far beyond those directly punished. Accountability here is shared across public security organs, local authorities, courts that fail to check abusive prosecutions, and Party disciplinary structures that ensure political loyalty overrides legal restraint.

A final harmful pattern is the routine use of national security as an all-purpose justification. This framing converts criticism, solidarity networks, and fact-finding into suspected threats to the state. It immunises repression from legal challenge and encourages officials to act aggressively because over-enforcement is politically safer than tolerance. The chief accountability lies with the central Communist Party leadership, which has made ideological discipline, security governance, and hostility to autonomous organisation defining features of the system. Over the past decade, the result has been the deliberate erosion of the informational and associational freedoms necessary for any meaningful public life outside Party control.
